title: Living ashtpadi 14

lines: A FEAST, OR A CARPENTER'S BREAD.
cards: Two invitations arrive in the same town on the same day. One is from a rich official, Malik Bhago, who is throwing a grand feast and expects every holy man around to attend.
The other is from Bhai Lalo, a carpenter, who can offer only plain, coarse bread. Guru Nanak is in town. Everyone assumes he'll go to the feast.
He goes to the carpenter's house. And when the insulted official demands to know why, the answer, as Sikhs tell it, becomes a moment in the janamsakhis, the old stories of Guru Nanak's life.

teach.h: MILK FROM ONE, BLOOD FROM THE OTHER.
teach.b: Here's how the story goes. Guru Nanak takes Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and a rich cake from Malik Bhago's feast in the other, and squeezes both. From Lalo's bread, the story says, comes milk.
From Bhago's, blood. Bhago's wealth had been squeezed out of the poor; Lalo's bread had been earned with his own hands.

teach.h: A STORY, HEARD AS A PICTURE.
teach.b: It's a story, told and retold, not a line from the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs hear it as a picture rather than a lab report. But the picture is exactly what the fourteenth ashtpadi has been saying.

Malik Bhago is siaanap made flesh: the clever official, working angles, rich from other people's labor, leaning on power and on people who could be bought. Lalo is the opposite: simple, straight, one hope.

Sikhs have a word for Lalo's kind of living: kirat, honest work. Kirat karni, earning by honest labor, is one of three duties Sikh teaching names together, alongside remembering the Name and sharing what you have.
It isn't glamorous. It's showing up, doing the job straight, charging a fair price, not cutting the corner when nobody would notice. And see what simplicity buys.
Malik Bhago has to keep track of his schemes, his debts, his flatterers.
Lalo has nothing to keep track of.
His bread is just bread. That's living ashtpadi fourteen: not becoming naive, but choosing, again and again, the way that needs no angles.

how: Sikhs tell the janamsakhi story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago to teach kirat karni, earning by honest work, one of the core Sikh duties along with remembering the Name and sharing.

o: charity given to a gurdwara kitchen
honest work, earning by your own labor
a craft passed down through a family

p: a rich official with a feast
old stories of Guru Nanak's life

s: the story of Lalo and Bhago comes from the janamsakhis, not the Guru Granth Sahib
it's a janamsakhi story, heard as a picture.
Guru Nanak accepted Malik Bhago's feast
he went to the carpenter Lalo's house instead.
kirat karni means earning money any way you can
it means earning by honest work.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak. a rich official invites you to a feast; a poor carpenter offers plain bread. where do you go?
games.why: the carpenter's. in the story, Lalo's bread gives milk and Bhago's cake gives blood: honest work against wealth squeezed from the poor.

practice: Think of something on your plate this week where there's a shortcut, a little angle, a convenient half-truth, and picture the angled way and how much tracking it would take.
Then picture the plain way, the honest email, the fair price, the work done properly, and feel how much lighter it is to carry. Choose it, here, quietly.

wordCard.voice: Kirat, honest work. Bhai Lalo's plain bread, the simple straight way that needs no angles and leaves nothing to keep track of.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kirat, work or labor; kirat karni is earning by honest work.

carryVoice: Your line: simple, straight. Plain bread is just bread, with nothing to keep track of. More tomorrow.
